situations.label: Sign-up
situations.title: A user signs up and creates an organization
situations.story: Tove signs in for the first time and creates Meadow Gardens. She has no seat in any tenant yet.
why: No tenant exists yet, so there is no tenant to begin in.
Tove has no seat, so no rights of hers can create a tenant.
`ProvisionAsync` accepts only system work outside any tenant. A handler that forgets the `using` is refused on its first request.
situations.actsIn: No tenant. `ProvisionAsync` then works inside the new tenant to save it.
situations.holds: Nothing in any tenant. Only `ProvisionAsync` accepts it.
situations.recordedDetail: Each event of the new tenant has `By`: the system, in the scope `tenancy`. The access history keeps these events.
situations.postgresDetail: The setting `tenancy.current_tenant` is empty, so the policies show the role no row. `ProvisionAsync` then starts system work inside the new tenant, so its save runs with that tenant set.
notes: Read `access.CurrentUser.Id` before the `using`. Inside it, `CurrentUser.IsSystem` is true and `Id` is null.
Put only the `ProvisionAsync` call inside the `using`.
Tove becomes the administrator. Her new seat is placed at the root and holds the administrators' role there.
A seat that calls `ProvisionAsync` gets `access.system-only`. A caller without a seat gets the refusal that tenant selection gave it.

situations.label: Staff create a tenant
situations.title: Your staff create a tenant for a customer
situations.story: A colleague in support signs in with an operator token. A customer calls in, and the colleague sets up South Docks for that customer, with the customer as its administrator.
why: An operator holds no seat, so every change an operator makes is operator work.
`[Operator]` says so on the request. The access check lets only operators through, and runs the handler as operator work.
The command has no `[ForTenant]` member, so the work acts in no tenant. Provisioning needs that.
situations.actsIn: No tenant. `ProvisionAsync` then works inside the new tenant to save it.
situations.recordedDetail: Each event of the new tenant has `By`: the operator, with the operator's id. That id is the current user's. A table of yours that calls `RecordsWhoChanged` gets `operator` in `CreatedByKind` and the id in `CreatedByIdentity`.
situations.postgresDetail: The command does not run as the operator's own database role. It runs as the scoped system role, as a sign-up does.
notes: A caller whose token carries no operator token role gets `tenancy.operators-only` from the access check. The handler does not run.
The handler calls no `Begin…` method. The operator work lasts for the whole handler.
The command names no tenant, so a `Tenant` header on the request is ignored.
The customer gets the administrator seat. The operator gets no seat.
code: [Operator]   // only operators; the handler runs as operator work in no tenant
public sealed record CreateCustomerTenant(string Slug, string Name, Guid Customer)
public async ValueTask<Tenant> Handle(CreateCustomerTenant command, CancellationToken cancellationToken)

situations.label: Staff change a tenant
situations.title: Your staff change a tenant
situations.story: The owner of Harbor Works asks support to suspend the tenant while they sort out a payment.
why: An operator has no seat in Harbor Works, so the change is operator work in that tenant.
The `[ForTenant]` member names the tenant on the command. The access check runs the handler as operator work there.
`SuspendAsync` accepts only system work in the tenant. Operator work is system work.
situations.actsIn: Harbor Works, the tenant the command names
situations.holds: Every permission in that tenant, for the whole handler
situations.recordedDetail: The event `tenancy.tenant-suspended` has `By`: the operator, with the operator's id. The access history keeps it. A table of yours that calls `RecordsWhoChanged` gets `operator` in `ChangedByKind` and the id in `ChangedByIdentity`.
situations.postgresDetail: `tenancy.current_tenant` holds Harbor Works. A query marked `[Operator]` starts no work, and reads every tenant through the database role that the operator's token role maps to.
notes: The whole handler holds every permission in Harbor Works and none in another tenant. Keep an operator's handler to the operator's act.
A request whose `Tenant` header names another tenant than the `[ForTenant]` member gets `tenancy.tenant-mismatch`.
`[Operator(Tenant = OperatorTenant.FromRequest)]` takes the tenant from the request's `Tenant` header instead. The command then has no `[ForTenant]` member.
A caller without an operator token role gets `tenancy.operators-only` before the handler runs.
code: [Operator]   // only operators; the handler runs as operator work in the tenant below
public sealed record SuspendTenant([ForTenant] TenantId Tenant, string Reason)
public async ValueTask<Tenant> Handle(SuspendTenant command, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
// A query starts no work. The operator reads every tenant through its own database role.

situations.label: Seeding
situations.title: Demo data is seeded at start-up
situations.story: On its first start in development, the host fills Harbor Works with units, seats and grants. Ada is the administrator of Harbor Works.
why: At start-up there is no request and no caller.
The work belongs inside one known tenant, Harbor Works.
`actingSeat` names Ada as the seat the work is for. The history then reads as system work for Ada.
situations.recordedAs: `system`; the events name the acting seat
situations.recordedDetail: Rhea's placement and grant name Ada as the seat that placed and granted them. The events' `By` is the system, for Ada. A table of yours that calls `RecordsWhoChanged` gets `system`, with no seat.
situations.postgresDetail: `tenancy.current_tenant` holds Harbor Works. The role cannot bypass row level security, so the policies keep the work in that tenant.
notes: The work holds every permission in Harbor Works and none in Meadow Gardens.
The last-administrator rule still applies. The seeding cannot take the administrators' role from Ada by mistake.
`actingSeat` adds no rights. It names the person the work is for, such as the administrator who starts an import.
A seeder runs in a service scope of its own. It resolves the managers and the access manager as a handler does.
code: public sealed class DemoSeeder(IServiceScopeFactory scopes) : IHostedService
await seats.PlaceAsync(rhea.Id, north.Id, primary: true, cancellationToken);

situations.label: Nightly job
situations.title: A nightly job visits every tenant
situations.story: Every night, the Inspections module closes the inspections that ran past their end date, in every tenant.
why: The job is the module's own work, so it runs in the module's scope, `inspections`.
The job first reads which tenants to visit. It then starts system work in each tenant in turn.
Each tenant gets its own `using`, so a mistake in one tenant cannot touch another.
situations.actsIn: Each tenant, one at a time
situations.holds: Every permission on the module's rows in each tenant. It reads Tenancy's tables and writes none.
situations.recordedDetail: A table of the module that calls `RecordsWhoChanged` gets `system` in its `…ByKind` columns. An event log names the system in the scope `inspections`.
situations.postgres: `ddd_system_in`, the module's scope, each tenant in turn
situations.postgresDetail: The role's claims carry the scope `inspections`. Work in a module's scope reads Tenancy's tables and cannot write them, so the job cannot change a seat or a grant.
notes: `TenantsToSweepAsync` returns the active and the suspended tenants. It reads them on a context of its own, so its read across tenants does not reach the job's work.
Call `TenantsToSweepAsync` before you start a transaction. It opens a connection of its own.
The Inspections module sees only Tenancy's ids. It gets `TenancyAccessManager` from one line, `[assembly: TenancyIds<TenantId, SeatId, OrganizationUnitId, RoleId>]`.
On a resource with members, Membership lets the work through where the resource's rules list the scope. By default the rules list the module's own scope.
code: foreach (var tenant in await access.TenantsToSweepAsync("inspections", cancellationToken))

situations.label: Grant after a condition
situations.title: Your code grants a role after a condition
situations.story: Leo passes the safety quiz. Harbor then gives him the role Safety officer at North, his unit. Nobody clicks a grant button.
why: Leo holds no `tenancy.grants.manage`, so his own seat cannot give the role.
Your handler checks the quiz as Leo. It then gives the role as system work.
Containment does not apply to system work, so the grant passes with containment on.
No person asked for the grant, so the work names no acting seat. The grant's reason says why the role was given.
situations.recordedDetail: The grant names no seat that granted it, and it stores the reason Passed Safety quiz. The event's `GrantedBy` is empty, and its `By` is the system in the scope `tenancy`.
situations.postgresDetail: Only work in the scope `tenancy` writes Tenancy's tables, so the grant uses Tenancy's scope.
notes: Leave out `actingSeat` here. It names the person who asked for the work. With Leo as acting seat, the history would read as system work for Leo, which looks as if Leo gave himself the role.
Take the tenant and the seat from `access.CurrentTenant`. Take the role and the unit from your own records. A role taken from the request would let anyone who passes name the administrators' role.
Only the `GrantAsync` call runs as system work. The quiz check runs as Leo.
The handler takes `SeatManager`, so it lives in a project that sees Tenancy's classes.

situations.label: Link with a token
situations.title: A link carries a token instead of a sign-in
situations.story: Rhea adds a calendar feed of her inspections to her phone. The calendar app fetches `/feeds/{token}.ics` without a sign-in. The token is the only proof.
why: Nobody signs in, so the request cannot run as Rhea.
Your code checks the token and finds the seat it belongs to.
Token work for that seat makes the history name the link and Rhea's seat.
situations.holds: Every row of the module in that tenant. Your code reads only the seat's rows.
situations.recordedAs: `token`, with the seat the token stands for
situations.recordedDetail: A table of the module that calls `RecordsWhoChanged` gets `token`, with no seat in the columns. An event log names the seat the token stands for.
situations.postgresDetail: The scope is required and is the module's, `inspections`. So the work cannot write Tenancy's tables.
notes: Token work is system work. It could read every inspection in the tenant, so your code reads only Rhea's.
Start it only after your code has checked the token and found that the seat is still in use.
The request is `[AllowAnonymous]`. The handler's check of the token is what lets the work through.
code: [AllowAnonymous]   // the link has no sign-in; the handler checks the token

situations.label: No Begin
situations.title: An administrator imports seats
situations.use: Nothing. The handler runs as the caller.
situations.story: Ada uploads a list of 40 people to give them seats at North.
why: Ada's seat holds `tenancy.seats.manage`, so the handler can do the work as Ada.
System work would skip Ada's checks for no reason.
With system work, the history would name the system instead of Ada.
situations.recordedDetail: The events' `By` is Ada's seat, and the access history keeps them. A table of yours that calls `RecordsWhoChanged` gets `seat`, and `…BySeat` holds Ada's seat.
situations.postgresDetail: `tenancy.current_tenant` holds Harbor Works, and the policies find Ada's seat again from her token.
notes: The managers check every new seat against Ada's rights, as for one seat added by hand.
A caller without `tenancy.seats.manage` gets `tenancy.not-permitted` from the access check.
Start system work only when the caller's own rights cannot do the work.
